```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(lstparsR)
```

## Overview

**lstparsR** reads NONMEM `.lst` listing files and extracts parameter
estimates into tidy tibbles. It is designed for population pharmacokinetic
and pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) workflows where many model runs need to be
parsed programmatically.

Key design choices:

- Parameter output is returned as tibbles with consistent column names.
- Missing optional quantities (e.g., standard errors when the covariance step
  is absent) are `NA`. Missing required parameter sections raise errors;
  `fetch_all()` catches these, warns, and returns `NULL` for failed elements.
- Both VECTOR blocks (THETA) and lower-triangular MATRIX blocks
  (OMEGA, SIGMA) are handled, including multi-line parameter sets.

## Reading a Listing File

Use `read_lst_file()` to load a `.lst` file into an S3 object of class
`"lst"`. The examples use synthetic listings that ship with the package
(see [Synthetic Example Listings](#synthetic-example-listings)); this one is
a FOCE-I run with a complete covariance step:

```{r read}
path <- system.file("extdata", "lst", "s01_focei_cov_success.lst",
                    package = "lstparsR")
lst  <- read_lst_file(path)
lst
summary(lst)
```

The `lst` object is simply a character vector (one element per line) with
class `"lst"` attached. All `fetch_*` functions require this class.

## Extracting THETA (Fixed Effects)

```{r thetas}
fetch_thetas(lst)
```

Each row corresponds to one THETA parameter. The `se` and `rse` columns
contain the standard error and relative standard error (as a percentage),
respectively.

Use the `digits` argument to round RSE values:

```{r thetas-rounded}
fetch_thetas(lst, digits = 1)
```

## Extracting OMEGA (Random Effects)

`fetch_etas()` extracts the diagonal of the OMEGA covariance matrix,
plus ETA shrinkage when reported:

```{r etas}
fetch_etas(lst)
```

Shrinkage values can be rounded separately:

```{r etas-rounded}
fetch_etas(lst, digits = 1, shk_digits = 1)
```

## Extracting SIGMA (Residual Error)

```{r sigmas}
fetch_sigmas(lst)
```

## Objective Function Value

```{r ofv}
fetch_ofv(lst)
```

For failed runs, `fetch_ofv()` falls back to the workflow footer
(`OFV = ...`) if the standard `#OBJV:` line is absent.

## Condition Number

The condition number is computed as the ratio of the largest to smallest
eigenvalue of the correlation matrix of parameter estimates. Values above
1000 suggest numerical instability:

```{r condn}
fetch_condn(lst)
```

## All at Once

`fetch_all()` runs every parser in a single call. Individual parser
failures are caught and returned as `NULL` with a warning, so a single
problematic section does not abort the entire extraction:

```{r fetch-all}
result <- fetch_all(lst)
names(result)
result$thetas
result$ofv
result$condn
```

## Runs Without a Covariance Step

When NONMEM did not run or complete a covariance step, SE, RSE,
and condition number are returned as `NA`:

```{r no-cov}
path2 <- system.file("extdata", "lst", "s39_focei_no_cov.lst",
                     package = "lstparsR")
lst2  <- read_lst_file(path2)
fetch_thetas(lst2)
fetch_condn(lst2)
```

## Synthetic Example Listings

The package ships 39 small, invented listings in `extdata/lst`, generated by
a script (`data-raw/make_synthetic_lst.R` in the source repository). Each
case exercises one estimation method, run outcome or layout feature, from a
successful FOCE-I run with a complete covariance step to aborted covariance
steps, chained `$ESTIMATION` records, wrapped parameter records and truncated
files. `manifest.csv` describes the cases and the values they contain:

```{r synthetic-manifest}
corpus   <- system.file("extdata", "lst", package = "lstparsR")
manifest <- read.csv(file.path(corpus, "manifest.csv"))
head(manifest[, c("case_id", "final_method", "covariance")])
```

Parsing a few of them side by side shows how unavailable quantities are
reported: standard errors and the condition number become `NA` when the
covariance step was aborted or not reached, and `fetch_all()` returns `NULL`
for parameter tables that a truncated listing does not contain.

```{r synthetic-batch}
cases <- c("s01", "s09", "s15", "s18", "s32")
files <- file.path(corpus, manifest$file[match(cases, manifest$case_id)])
runs  <- lapply(files, function(f) suppressWarnings(fetch_all(read_lst_file(f))))
data.frame(
  case       = cases,
  covariance = manifest$covariance[match(cases, manifest$case_id)],
  thetas     = vapply(runs, function(r) NROW(r$thetas), integer(1)),
  se_th1     = vapply(runs, function(r) if (is.null(r$thetas)) NA else r$thetas$se[1], numeric(1)),
  ofv        = vapply(runs, function(r) r$ofv, numeric(1)),
  condn      = round(vapply(runs, function(r) r$condn, numeric(1)), 2)
)
```

## Batch Processing

A common pattern is to parse many `.lst` files at once:

```{r batch, eval = FALSE}
library(purrr)

lst_files <- list.files("models/", pattern = "\\.lst$", full.names = TRUE)

results <- map(lst_files, \(f) {
  lst <- read_lst_file(f)
  fetch_all(lst)
})

# Combine all THETA tables
all_thetas <- map_dfr(results, "thetas", .id = "run")
```

## Estimation Headers and Output Layouts

lstparsR recognizes the following NONMEM estimation method headers:

- First Order (FO)
- First Order Conditional Estimation (FOCE)
- First Order Conditional Estimation with Interaction (FOCE-I)
- Laplacian Conditional Estimation, with or without interaction (LAPLACE)
- Iterative Two Stage (ITS)
- Stochastic Approximation Expectation-Maximization (SAEM)
- Importance Sampling (IMP), including evaluation-only steps
- Importance Sampling Assisted by Mode A Posteriori (IMPMAP)
- MCMC Bayesian Analysis (BAYES)

Numerical regression tests cover FOCE-I listings, controlled edge cases and
a synthetic corpus of invented listings for every method above (see
`extdata/lst/manifest.csv`); FO listings have additional execution coverage.
The synthetic layouts of the EM and Bayesian methods follow the NONMEM 7
documentation. Recognizing a method header does not validate every layout or
posterior summary from that method. The parsers
expect the fixed-format result sections shown in the examples. Compare results
with the original listing for unfamiliar layouts. Parsing does not validate the
scientific model or its estimates.

## Interactive Exploration

For interactive use, launch the built-in Shiny application:

```{r shiny, eval = FALSE}
lstparsR::run_app()
```

This opens a browser-based interface where you can upload `.lst` files,
view parsed results in tables, and download them as CSV or RDS.
